article_ideas.audience: Agent platform engineers and engineering leads deciding what to instrument before launch
article_ideas.based_on: Every continual learning company is an observability company.
article_ideas.thesis: Continual learning for agents is indistinguishable from observability work: teams that treat tracing as an ops add-on added after the agent works have foreclosed their own improvement loop, because the trace stream is the raw input to every later adaptation. project_ideas.based_on: What is the true crossover point where fine-tuned open models on owned hardware beat frontier-model token pricing

project_ideas.name: Trace-Judge Cost Crossover Bench
project_ideas.poc: Build one judge task with a fixed rubric, run it through a frontier API judge and a fine-tuned open judge over increasing volumes, and chart total cost of ownership (fine-tuning hours, cluster/hosting, ops) against per-token API spend at matched quality.

project_ideas.based_on: When has a harness actually hit its ceiling, signaling it is time to fine-tune?
project_ideas.hypothesis: Marginal task-success improvement per harness iteration decays predictably before a fine-tuning cycle is warranted, so the decay curve can be used as a switch signal between harness engineering and fine-tuning.
project_ideas.measurement: Correlation between measured marginal gain per iteration and the observed benefit of the subsequent fine-tuning cycle across several task suites.
project_ideas.name: Harness Saturation Meter
project_ideas.poc: Instrument an agent improvement loop to record every harness change with its evaluation delta and wall-clock feedback latency, then test whether a flattening marginal-gain curve precedes the point where a fine-tuning cycle produces the next significant gain.

project_ideas.based_on: You cannot have continual learning without traces, and tracing provides the raw data needed for agent adaptation.
project_ideas.hypothesis: Teams that commit to a durable trace schema and retention policy at first deployment can later run adaptation loops that teams adding logging post-hoc cannot, and the difference is visible in how quickly they can reconstruct dense labels from historical runs.
project_ideas.measurement: Fraction of historical runs convertible into usable supervision, time to first mined improvement loop, and storage cost per retained run.
project_ideas.name: Trace Retention Contract
project_ideas.poc: Instrument two agents — one with day-one full-fidelity trace capture plus schema, one with logging added after it works — then attempt the same trace-derived label-mining task against each history and compare how much usable supervision can be reconstructed.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Vivek Trivedy
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Continual learning and agent improvement through data mining and tracing
  • Purpose: To explain how data mining over agent traces, observability, and continual learning drive agent improvement and cost efficiency. Vivek Trivedy from LangChain discusses how improving AI agents over time is fundamentally a data mining problem. He outlines a recipe for building, running, and improving agents by collecting traces, data mining, and running experiments. He explores the challenges of reading traces at scale, leveraging open-source models for cost-efficient trace judging, and drawing parallels between machine learning and agent harness engineering.

Topic Map

The Recipe for Continuously Improving Agents

  • Explanation: A four-step recipe for building and improving agents: ship a v1 agent, collect traces, data mine the traces, and run experiments.
  • Key claims:
    • No one knows what an agent will do until they run it.
    • Agents trade determinism for autonomy.
    • Every continual learning company is an observability company.
  • Examples:
    • Running an agent, collecting traces from tool calls, output messages, API calls, and CLI usage.
  • Terminology:
    • Traces
    • Observability
    • Continual Learning
    • Data Mining
  • Why it matters: Provides a systematic framework for moving from initial agent deployment to data-driven iterative improvement.

Why Reading Traces at Scale is Hard

  • Explanation: Discusses the challenges of handling massive volumes of trace data generated by long-horizon agents.
  • Key claims:
    • Reading traces at scale is super expensive.
    • Traces don't fit in context windows.
    • Modern agent runs can be millions of tokens long.
  • Examples:
    • Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, or deep agents producing massive trace files.
  • Terminology:
    • Trace Data
    • Context Window
    • Token Cost
    • Long-Horizon Agents
  • Why it matters: Highlights why naive approaches to reviewing all agent traces fail and necessitates specialized tools like LangSmith Engine.

Open Models for Cost-Efficient Trace Judges

  • Explanation: Explores using open-source models (like DeepSeek or Llama models) instead of frontier models to judge traces at a lower cost.
  • Key claims:
    • Open models have hidden inflection points in intelligence.
    • Fine-tuning open models can match or exceed frontier performance on specific tasks at a fraction of the cost.
    • Moving from token costs to hardware cluster costs for high-inference workloads.
  • Examples:
    • Using Opus vs. open models on the Harvey legal benchmark.
  • Terminology:
    • Open Models
    • Fine-Tuning
    • Harness Engineering
    • Trace Judging
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates how teams can dramatically reduce the cost of trace evaluation and agent supervision.

Fitting Systems to Data: The Model-Harness-Task Fit

  • Explanation: Draws an analogy between classical machine learning (Scikit-learn estimators) and modern agent engineering.
  • Key claims:
    • Agent engineering parallels classical machine learning fit methods.
    • The process involves Model + Harness + Task fit.
    • Auto-research and auto-feedback loops are central to agent optimization.
  • Examples:
    • Scikit-learn fit method applied to models, harnesses, and tasks.
  • Terminology:
    • Model-Harness-Task Fit
    • Auto-Research
    • Fit Functions
    • Distillation
  • Why it matters: Bridges traditional ML engineering paradigms with modern LLM agent development.

Key Points

Observability and Continual Learning are tightly coupled

  • Explanation: You cannot have continual learning without traces, and tracing provides the raw data needed for agent adaptation.
  • Evidence: Agents produce trace data during environment execution, which feeds human or automated learning loops.
  • Practical implication: Teams must prioritize robust tracing and logging infrastructure from day one of agent deployment.

Harness Engineering vs. Fine-Tuning

  • Explanation: Harness engineering provides fast feedback loops, while fine-tuning helps scale intelligence once harness limits are reached.
  • Evidence: Harness engineering gives feedback in minutes; fine-tuning optimizes base models for specific vertical tasks.
  • Practical implication: Use a sandwich approach: start with harness engineering, fine-tune to break ceilings, and continue harness engineering.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Recipe for Continuously Improving Agents

  • How it works: A linear pipeline moving from deployment to data extraction and experimentation.
  • Components:
    • Build a v1 agent and start running it
    • Collect lots of traces
    • Curate the trace data (data mining)
    • Run experiments on your data
  • When to use: When deploying autonomous agents in production that need iterative improvement.

Model-Harness-Task Fit

  • How it works: Adapting learning systems to data similar to classical ML estimator fitting.
  • Components:
    • Model
    • Harness
    • Task
    • Fit Function
  • When to use: When optimizing agent performance across specific enterprise domains.

Examples & Case Studies

Running agents on terminal bench tasks and analyzing traces.

  • Illustrates: How terminal bench outputs binary pass/fail results, requiring densified feedback signals from traces to guide improvement.
  • Lesson: Traces provide the granular behavioral data needed to understand why an agent succeeded or failed.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Turn on tracing for your agents immediately to capture behavioral data.
    • Use open-source models for trace judging and evaluation to reduce costs.
  • Strategic:
    • Treat agent improvement as a data mining and continual learning pipeline.
    • Balance harness engineering and model fine-tuning based on performance ceilings and cost.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do we scale sleep-time compute and memory management for long-horizon agents?
    • How can we automate the densification of feedback signals from agent traces?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Modern agent runs will soon exceed all human lifetime data production. (projection)
  • Fine-tuning open models can match frontier model trace judging capabilities at 1-2 orders of magnitude lower cost. (benchmark claim)

Notable Quotes

"Improving Agents is a Data Mining Problem." (at 0:25) "Every Continual Learning Company is an Observability Company." (at 3:42) "No one knows what their agent will do until they run it. Agents trade determinism for autonomy." (at 5:26)

Compressed Summary

  • Agent improvement is fundamentally a data mining problem over trace logs.
  • Traces at scale present cost and context window challenges.
  • Open models offer cost-efficient alternatives for trace judging and fine-tuning.
  • Continual learning requires integrating observational trace data back into agent state and harnesses.
  • Keywords: agents, traces, observability, continual-learning, fine-tuning
  • Core insight: Improving autonomous AI agents at scale requires treating trace data collection, mining, and continual learning as a unified engineering pipeline.

## Key Points
### Observability and Continual Learning are tightly coupled
- **Explanation**: You cannot have continual learning without traces, and tracing provides the raw data needed for agent adaptation.
- **Evidence**: Agents produce trace data during environment execution, which feeds human or automated learning loops.
- **Practical implication**: Teams must prioritize robust tracing and logging infrastructure from day one of agent deployment.
### Harness Engineering vs. Fine-Tuning
- **Explanation**: Harness engineering provides fast feedback loops, while fine-tuning helps scale intelligence once harness limits are reached.
- **Evidence**: Harness engineering gives feedback in minutes; fine-tuning optimizes base models for specific vertical tasks.
- **Practical implication**: Use a sandwich approach: start with harness engineering, fine-tune to break ceilings, and continue harness engineering.
